question: Why is MinMax scaling described as mandatory rather than optional for KNN, and what would happen if you skipped it on a dataset with income and age columns?
The bank marketing example found k=1 to be the best-performing value. Why does the notebook treat this as a warning sign rather than a good result?
How does the nested cross-validation setup in the newer knn.py code work (outer vs. inner loop), and what specific problem does it fix?
Which R functions from the original KNN lab map to sklearn's MinMaxScaler and KNeighborsClassifier, and what does the conversion note say about getting sensitivity and specificity in Python?
KNN requires scaling and one-hot encoding before fitting. How do decision trees differ on these preprocessing requirements, and why does that difference exist?
The KNN dataset has only ~11.6% positive cases. How do the confusion matrix concepts introduced here connect to the fairness metrics discussed on the ML bias page?
Which R function does the DS-3021 decision tree material map to Python's `cost_complexity_pruning_path`, and what practical difference does the page note between the two?
Which slide deck is this decision-trees page built from, and why does the page warn students to check which deck was used in a given semester?
Why does recursive binary splitting make decision trees unstable and only locally optimal, rather than globally optimal?
How does information gain get computed in the 'should you play outside?' example — what role does the weighting of child-node entropies play?
Why does the DT class lab explicitly tell students not to scale the data, when the KNN lab insists on scaling?
How does the instability weakness of a single decision tree connect to what's covered in the ensemble methods lecture in week 12?
What is the historical lineage from CART to C5.0, and which of these algorithms does sklearn's `DecisionTreeClassifier` implement?
How do Equality of Odds, Equal Opportunity, and Demographic Parity differ, and why is Demographic Parity considered crude?

Why does the lecture re-derive confusion matrices and ROC/AUC before introducing the fairness metrics, and how does the fraud-detection toy example (135 emails, 50% threshold) illustrate the threshold tradeoff?
How does the class imbalance issue flagged on the k-NN and decision tree pages connect to the fairness metrics discussed here?
The page says the fairlearn example file is only a two-line import stub — what materials would I need to look at instead to work through a runnable fairness or confusion-matrix example?
Why did YouTube's 2011-12 shift from optimizing clicks to optimizing watch-time push viewers toward more extreme content, and why does the page say this wasn't a 'bug'?
What are the pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing interventions described in the companion Value_1.pptx deck?
In the bank-marketing KNN worked example, what are the confusion matrix counts and what recall does the model achieve on the positive class?
Why does the course recommend F1 over accuracy for the bank marketing dataset, given that accuracy is 88.8%?
How does log loss punish a confident wrong prediction compared to an uncertain one, and what numbers does the course's worked table give?
The 135-email fraud example reappears in the week 14 bias lecture — how does the confusion-matrix machinery on this page set up the fairness metrics on [[course/ml-bias]]?
Why is AUC described as the right metric for comparing two models, while precision and recall are not?
How do the evaluation metrics on this page fit into the nested cross-validation rewrite described on [[course/knn]]?
What Python calls replace R's confusionMatrix() and the ROCR prediction()/performance() pair, and why does the conversion table list several Python functions for one R function?
What split criterion does a regression tree use instead of Gini or entropy, and how is it computed in the slides' worked example with values 75, 85, and 80?
Why does a regression tree leaf predict the arithmetic mean of the training targets that land there rather than some other summary statistic?
When passing a list of scoring metrics to GridSearchCV for a DecisionTreeRegressor, why does scikit-learn require you to set `refit`, and why do MSE/MAE come back as negative numbers?
In the wine-quality lecture notebook, what was the best max_depth and what were the test-set R², RMSE, and MAE?

Why does the Pipeline + ColumnTransformer version of the wine example, which imputes medians inside each CV fold, end up doing worse on the test set than the simpler drop-NA version — and why does the notebook treat that as a discussion point rather than a bug?

Which parts of the CART workflow described on [[course/decision-trees]] carry over unchanged to regression trees, and which specific steps in the week 9 lab replace the classification lab's confusion-matrix work?
Why can't k-means' k be chosen by cross-validated accuracy the way KNN's k is, and what does the course use instead?
How does the house-votes example demonstrate 'validation after the fact,' and why isn't party affiliation given to the algorithm during clustering?
What does k mean in KNN versus k-means, and what prerequisite do both methods share because they're distance-based?
How does the NBA clustering lab mirror the in-class house-votes workflow, and what plays the role that party affiliation played there?
Which slide deck version is treated as canonical for this topic, and what content does it add over the 2021 PDF?
Why does the page say variance explained rising from ≈0.719 at k=2 to ≈0.795 at k=3 doesn't mean k=3 is a better choice?
What are the three main tuning parameters of a Random Forest as taught in DS-3021, and what does each control?
In the lecture notebook's pregnancy/shopper example, what happened to OOB error as n_estimators was swept from 100 to 1000?
Why does sampling rows with replacement leave about a third of the training data unused per tree, and how does Random Forest exploit that to produce an OOB error estimate?
The slides describe random feature subsetting per split as 'kinda boosting' that reduces bias — why does the page say decorrelation is the better explanation?
How do MDI and permutation feature importance differ, and when would you prefer permutation importance?
Random Forest gives up what the decision-trees page calls a single tree's biggest advantage — what is it, and what tools does the course use to compensate?
Which R randomForest() outputs have no direct sklearn equivalent, and how does the course reconstruct them in Python?

The KNN page says feature scaling is mandatory, while the decision tree lab explicitly tells students NOT to scale. Explain why these two pieces of course guidance are consistent, and say which of the two rules applies to k-means clustering and why.
Trace the ~11.6% positive-rate bank-marketing dataset across the wiki: which pages reference it, and what conclusion does each draw about model evaluation from that imbalance?
The KNN lecture found k=1 was best. What problem does that flag, what specific fix does the current KNN codebase use, and where else in the course does that same fix (or its shallower cousin) appear?

Sensitivity and specificity are defined on at least three pages. Compare how [[course/knn]], [[course/ml-eval-metrics]], and [[course/ml-bias]] each use these two quantities, and explain how the fairness metrics build on them.
Decision trees are described as unstable and only locally optimal. Which later week's topic is presented as the direct fix, and by what two randomization mechanisms does it achieve that?
What does 'k' mean in KNN versus k-means, and how does the method of choosing k differ between the two? Name the specific selection techniques used in each course week.

Across KNN, decision trees, evaluation metrics, decision-tree regression, and ensembles, the wiki repeatedly documents an R→Python conversion pattern. Give three concrete examples where one R function call maps to multiple Python calls, drawn from at least three different pages.

Variable importance is handled differently for KNN, single decision trees, and Random Forest. Describe each approach and explain why permutation importance shows up in both the KNN and Random Forest material.

Class imbalance is flagged as a problem on the KNN, decision-trees, ml-eval-metrics, and ml-bias pages. Summarize the distinct concern each page raises about it, and explain how the accuracy problem becomes a fairness problem.

The wiki mentions leakage-safe preprocessing in at least two places (imputation inside a Pipeline, and nested cross-validation). Explain the shared underlying principle and cite the specific example from each page.

Several pages carry version or currency warnings — multiple slide decks, superseded PDFs, incomplete code stubs, or repo-vs-local lab differences. List these caveats and identify which pages they appear on.

The k-means in-class code feeds cluster labels into a DecisionTreeClassifier. Explain what this demonstrates about the relationship between the week 10 unsupervised material and the week 8 supervised material, and how the resulting models are compared.

Chart the DS-3021 week numbers for KNN, evaluation metrics, decision trees, decision-tree regression, k-means clustering, ensemble methods, and ML bias, and explain how the ordering reflects a deliberate build-up of prerequisites.

Compare how model performance is validated when there is no held-out labeled target: contrast the out-of-bag error estimate in Random Forest with the after-the-fact validation strategy used in k-means clustering, and note what role a held-out label plays in each.
